Both of my checks came back against the goal idea, so I'm dropping it as I said I would. " want" gets only 1% at the first "We" (" are" has 99%), so it isn't a natural branch. The goal-mention effect also disappears within step strata (-1.5 ± 4.7 points). The final answer equals the last computed value in about 70% of wrong answers in both registers, and gold is derived but unreported in only 10-16%, so reporting the wrong quantity is a minor failure. That leaves first-line question overlap (+9.1 ± 3.5) as the only hint still standing, and it's correlational.

Before spending more on that, I should finish a line I left half-tested. E3 was the only edit with a significant positive signal: word tokens +0.21 ± 0.06, and arithmetic logprob +0.007 ± 0.001. Small per-token gains could add up over a whole solution, and ×1.5 may simply be too weak. So I'll test a higher dose, ×2.5 on heads 2 and 3 of L17, on the same text set as passes 7 and 8. That also gives the several-strengths evidence the method asks for.

First, a free comparison: how did the h0 boost (E2) affect word tokens on the shared 450 references? If raising h0 hurt where raising h2/h3 helped, then this is really a rebalancing effect between heads. In the next pass, effects that scale with dose would support a real rebalancing effect, while gains that plateau or reverse, with retrieval costs growing, would close this line.

E2 and E3 turn out to be close to mirror images, which is what a rebalancing between heads should look like. Raising h0 lowers logprob on result digits (-0.019), `othernum_first` (-0.060) and word tokens (-0.003), and raising h2/h3 improved all three (+0.014, +0.032, +0.003). Top-1 accuracy tells the same story more weakly. So there's a real axis of head share here, and the question is how far it goes. E3b, at ×2.5 on h2 and h3, is saved as the only active edit and the plan is in my notes. This pass uses the same 1,011 texts as passes 7 and 8. A dose effect would show up as result-digit and word gains that grow, while retrieval classes tell me what it costs.

The pass is done, so I'll run the same comparison against the pass 7 baseline and put the ×1.5 and ×2.5 results next to each other. What I care about is whether result-digit, sum and word gains keep growing with dose and what retrieval pays for them. A monotonic gain with a small retrieval cost would justify a generation pass.

The dose test closes this line by the criterion I set. Going from ×1.5 to ×2.5, the word-token logprob gain reversed (+0.0029 to -0.0021) and retrieval costs roughly tripled (`fromproblem_later` -0.010 to -0.028, `fromearlier_later` -0.005 to -0.016). Overall result accuracy stays within noise at +0.21 ± 0.27, and +3 sums gain 4.2 ± 2.2 points while +2 sums lose 0.9 ± 0.5. So the operand-head axis is a trade-off with its best point near ×1.5, not an unexploited gain.

I'll still give ×1.5 one generation pass at some point, because teacher-forced tokens can't show register-level effects, as E4 proved. The bigger question right now is different. Accuracy on Let answers to two-step problems, by far the easiest ones, is only about 40%, so 60% of them fail with almost no chain length to go wrong. Whatever breaks there is the cleanest view of the failure, and I haven't looked at it separately.

I'll drop the active edit and profile two-step failures: cut-offs, false equations, missing numbers and how many more equations the model writes than the reference needs. I'll also read a few cases. A single dominant pattern, such as overcomplicating easy problems, would be a much better target than anything so far. If they just look like the general failure in miniature, I'll go to generation on E3.
